case_study_insert.main_stem: Norwood Valley Preserves (NVP) is a private limited company in the food processing sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Ines Norwood, the business makes fruit preserves and chutneys for regional grocery chains and independent supermarkets, and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. NVP plans to invest $720,000 in an automated glass-jar filling line with recyclable eco-packaging, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.80 a unit and a selling price of $10.80, and currently produces 96,000 units a year. NVP faces rising warehouse waste and an increase in customer quality complaints about jar seals.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The preserves line filled 24,000 jars last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 3.6% a year earlier. Customer complaints about seals fell from 44 to 19 per month. Average order fulfilment is 4.1 days. A survey of 500 shoppers found that 62% would pay up to $0.50 more for recyclable eco-packaging, and 48% check jar recycling labels before buying. A skills audit shows 18 of 60 staff have not been trained on the new filling machines; off-the-job courses at the college cost $850 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Norwood Valley Preserves for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.40 to $14.14 per hour from April 2026, lifting total wage bills. (3) Glass and packaging input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year, while consumer spending on preserves grew 2.8% over the same period.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for NVP of using retained profit to fund the glass-jar filling line instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $270,000 of retained profit costs NVP nothing in interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when it already carries $240,000 of fixed costs a year. With the base interest rate at 5.75%, servicing a $450,000 bank loan would add a substantial interest burden, whereas internally funded money lets every dollar of the $5.00 contribution on each jar stay in the business to absorb the 9.5% rise in glass and packaging costs. This matters for a preserves maker selling at $10.80 to regional grocery chains that resist price increases.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk attached to a bank loan, so Ines Norwood's $720,000 automated filling line is not jeopardised if demand for chutneys disappoints. It also keeps ownership and control inside the founder's private limited company: no lender can impose conditions on how the recyclable eco-packaging line is run, and no outside party gains a claim on future profits, which suits NVP's hierarchical, autocratic style where the founder retains tight control of strategy and of the warehouse waste problem.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should NVP choose to promote its new jar range? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A TV campaign would build awareness of NVP's recyclable glass-jar preserves across all the regional grocery chains and independent supermarkets at once. However, airtime and production costs are very high relative to a 60-staff business funding a $720,000 line, and much of a national audience would never see the product on a local shelf, so a large share of the spend would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is much cheaper and reaches the regional catchment where NVP's preserves are actually stocked, and it suits short messages about the $0.50 eco-packaging premium. Its weakness is narrow reach: with output of 96,000 jars a year aimed at several chains, local listeners alone cannot shift enough volume, and audio cannot show the recyclable jar and recycling label that 48% of shoppers check.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and family influencers can demonstrate the jar, the seal quality and the recyclable eco-packaging directly to the 62% of 500 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.50 more, and engagement is measurable at low cost per reached shopper. Results build more slowly than television and depend on influencer credibility, but the message travels nationally without TV-scale budgets.

Recommendation: NVP should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets exactly the segment identified in the research, shows the packaging that 48% of buyers inspect, and costs far less than television while reaching beyond radio's local audience. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 60-employee company servicing a $450,000 loan; radio is rejected as too narrow for 96,000 units of national-chain supply. NVP should support influencers with modest in-store shelf promotions.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to NVP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of NVP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of NVP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for NVP of introducing democratic leadership to tackle its rising warehouse waste and quality complaints.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 60 staff a real voice in how the automated filling line and warehouse are organised, which helps satisfy social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Workers who handle seals every shift can suggest practical fixes to the jar-sealing routine that caused the 2.4% defect rate, so quality complaints about seals should fall. Because they help design the change, staff are more likely to follow the new procedures consistently, directly reducing the warehouse waste that is currently rising.

Point 2: Involving employees in decisions raises commitment and reduces the likelihood of staff leaving, protecting the 96,000-unit output while the $720,000 line beds in. Their ideas can target the 18 staff still untrained on the filling machines, making any $850 college training more effective because workers themselves identify the real skill gaps. For an autocratic founder like Ines Norwood, consultation also supplies local information she cannot see from the top of a hierarchical structure, leading to better waste-reduction decisions and fewer dissatisfied customers than a purely top-down instruction would achieve.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college for the 18 staff. Which should NVP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the filling line is directly relevant to NVP's own machines and seal-quality standards, costs no course fees, and keeps the 18 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 24,000 jars filled last quarter and the improvement to a 2.4% defect rate. The drawbacks are that trainer-operators have less time for their own work, bad habits may be passed on, and there is no formal certificate if grocery chains ask for records of machine competence.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $850 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate for all 18 staff, costing $15,300 in total — small beside the $720,000 investment. It removes workers from the line, however, cutting short-term capacity when 96,000 units are needed, and generic content may not match NVP's exact sealing settings, so follow-up coaching on site would still be required.

Decision: NVP should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, with short college sessions later for the most senior operators. It is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids losing output while waste and seal complaints are already problems; full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing 18 of 60 staff and spending $15,300 would disrupt supermarket deliveries, and college visits can be added once the new line stabilises.

Additional considerations: The falling defect rate of 2.4% and the drop in seal complaints from 44 to 19 a month show that current practices are improving, so disrupting the line with a full college intake could undo this progress. NVP could blend both methods: brief college induction for each of the 18 staff followed by supervised practice on the filling machines, spreading the $850 cost over time while keeping output close to 96,000 units.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to NVP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of NVP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of NVP with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NVP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 48,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 96,000-unit output; pricing and discount modelling against $240,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $720,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $8.30 with labour productivity of 1,600 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($10.80 − $5.80) = $240,000 ÷ $5.00 = 48,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 48,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $10.80 − $5.80 = $5.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NVP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 48,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 96,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 48,000 units, to judge whether the $720,000 filling line is justified.
2. Contribution of $5.00 lets managers model a supermarket discount: a $0.50 price cut to $10.30 leaves $4.50 contribution, showing how much extra volume is needed to cover $240,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs and contribution helps set the volume needed to service the $450,000 bank loan before committing further capital.
4. Unit cost of $240,000 ÷ 96,000 + $5.80 = $8.30 and productivity of 96,000 ÷ 60 = 1,600 units per worker let managers benchmark weekly performance and target the warehouse waste problem.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NVP's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Which ratio provides the stronger evidence of improvement? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 20.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 24.0%

Detailed workings: In 2024 gross profit of $1,470,000 came from revenue $4,200,000 less cost of sales $2,730,000; $1,470,000 ÷ $4,200,000 = 35.0%. In 2025 gross profit of $2,016,000 = revenue $5,040,000 − cost of sales $3,024,000; $2,016,000 ÷ $5,040,000 = 40.0%. Operating profit rose from $630,000 to $1,008,000; $630,000 ÷ $4,200,000 = 15.0% and $1,008,000 ÷ $5,040,000 = 20.0%. Capital employed moved from $3,500,000 to $4,200,000; $630,000 ÷ $3,500,000 = 18.0% and $1,008,000 ÷ $4,200,000 = 24.0%. Interest payable was $90,000 then $120,000.

Evaluation: Every measure improved, so profitability strengthened. Gross profitability rose from 35.0% to 40.0%, suggesting better control of jar and ingredient costs relative to sales, helped by the falling 2.4% defect rate. The operating return on sales climbed from 15.0% to 20.0%, showing the $240,000 fixed-cost base is being spread over more output. Return on capital rose from 18.0% to 24.0% even though the asset base grew to $4,200,000 to fund the $720,000 line, so the new investment is already earning.

Stronger evidence: the profit margin, because it gained five percentage points and directly reflects operating efficiency from the given revenue and cost figures, whereas the return on capital is also influenced by the enlarged capital base.

Conclusion: NVP's financial performance has clearly improved. All three margins rose, with the operating return on sales giving the clearest signal; the main caution is that rising interest payable and the $450,000 loan still have to be serviced.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements, and a justified conclusion naming the stronger evidence.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NVP of introducing recyclable eco-packaging for its preserves range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recyclable eco-packaging matches the 62% of 500 surveyed shoppers who would pay up to $0.50 more, letting NVP protect its $5.00 contribution per unit even while glass and packaging input costs rise 9.5%. It also strengthens the brand with the 48% who check jar recycling labels, helping retain listings with regional grocery chains and independent supermarkets for the $720,000 filling line.

Disadvantage: Sustainable materials usually cost more than standard jars, which would push up the $5.80 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the full $0.50 premium is accepted across the whole range. Any failure in the new eco-materials, such as weaker seals or shorter shelf life, would raise the 2.4% defect rate and the customer complaints about seals, adding waste before the automated line has stabilised and making the $450,000 loan harder to service. With $270,000 retained profit already committed to the $720,000 line, preserving the $5.00 contribution is a priority for covering that loan.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in glass and packaging input costs will affect NVP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate (5.0% to 5.75%): If NVP's $450,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.0075 × $450,000 = $3,375 a year. That is modest against $240,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher base rates could also make future borrowing for the $720,000 line dearer and make consumers more cautious about premium preserves, but NVP can cap this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage (5.5%, to $14.14 from $13.40 per hour): With a workforce of 60 in packing and warehouse roles, this feeds into wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no honest annual total can be invented; the defensible test is productivity of 96,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 1,600 units per worker. If output per worker holds, the rise is absorbable; if it slips, unit labour cost rises and the $5.00 contribution shrinks.

Input cost inflation (9.5% glass and packaging): The insert does not decompose the $5.80 variable cost, so only a bound can be computed: if all of it rose 9.5%, that adds 9.5% × $5.80 = $0.55 per unit; across 96,000 units that is about $52,800 a year (96,000 × $0.55). Only part can be recovered through the $0.50 eco-packaging premium, while spending on preserves grew just 2.8%.

Conclusion: The 9.5% input-cost rise has the greatest impact because it compounds on every one of the 96,000 jars and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that underpins the $720,000 investment. The interest effect is small and fixable, and the wage rise can be offset if productivity holds, whereas input inflation strikes the core unit economics with little pricing room.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to NVP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on NVP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of NVP with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.
